new_note: *And it shall manifestly appear to all nations and kings that they are no gods, but the works of men’s hands, and that there is no work of Yahuah (God) in them.* (Baruch 6:51). *And there ye shall serve gods, the work of men’s hands, wood and stone, which neither see, nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.* (Deuteronomy 4:28). Moses told Yashar'el (Israel) ahead of time what exile would look like: scattered among the nations, they would serve gods that were the work of men's hands, blind and deaf and lifeless. The letter in Baruch is written from inside that exile, in Babylon, where the gods are exactly what Moses described, wood overlaid with silver and gold. What Deuteronomy gave as the curse for forsaking the covenant, Baruch watches play out, and he points at the idols and says what Moses said: there is no work of Yahuah (God) in them. The exile was never only a change of address; it was being handed over to the very idols that cannot see or hear, until the people would know the difference and come home.
member_note: Baruch 6:51 — *they are no gods, but the works of men’s hands.* The exile curse Moses named in Deuteronomy 4:28, watched from inside Babylon.

new_note: *If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and Yahuah (God) shall give her to you.* (Ecclesiasticus 1:26). *Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear Elohim (God), and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.* (Ecclesiastes 12:13). Sirach puts wisdom on the far side of the commandments: keep them, and Yahuah (God) gives her. Solomon ends his whole book in the same place, fear Elohim (God) and keep his commandments, and calls that the whole duty of man. Neither writer knows a wisdom that stands apart from the commandments or a fear of Yahuah (God) that outgrows them. The commandments are not the beginner's course a wise man leaves behind; they are the door wisdom comes through, and the conclusion the wisest man in Yashar'el (Israel) arrived at.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 1:26 — *If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments.* Solomon's conclusion of the whole matter, in one line (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

new_note: *Distrust not the fear of Yahuah (God) when you are poor: and come not to him with a double heart.* (Ecclesiasticus 1:28). *And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir: and went not.* (Matthew 21:30). The second son in the parable says yes with his mouth and no with his feet. Sirach had already named that man: the one who comes to Yahuah (God) with a double heart, one heart for what he says and another for what he does. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the parable to the chief priests and elders, who had answered the Father's call through John with the words of obedience and none of the walking, and the double heart is what he is exposing. A yes that does not go is not a weaker obedience; it is the thing Sirach warns against, and the Father does not receive it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 1:28 — *come not to him with a double heart.* The second son's *I go, sir: and went not* (Matthew 21:30).

new_note: *Distrust not the fear of Yahuah (God) when you are poor: and come not to him with a double heart.* (Ecclesiasticus 1:28). *Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.* (Matthew 23:25). A double heart is a clean outside and a different inside. Sirach warns the one who comes to Yahuah (God) not to come that way; Yahusha (Jesus) names the religious leadership of his day as having done exactly that, the cup scrubbed where men can see and full of extortion and excess where only Elohim (God) sees. The two verses are the same diagnosis from two directions, the counsel before the fault and the woe after it. Yahuah (God) has always looked on the heart, so a system that polishes the outside and leaves the inside alone has misjudged who is doing the inspecting.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 1:28 — *come not to him with a double heart.* The clean cup with the foul inside at Matthew 23:25.

new_note: *Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men, and take good heed what you speak.* (Ecclesiasticus 1:29). *And he came to the second, and said likewise. And he answered and said, I go, sir: and went not.* (Matthew 21:30). Sirach's warning is against being a hypocrite in the sight of men, and against careless speech, and the second son in the parable fails both at once. He speaks the right words, I go, sir, where men can hear them, and then does not go. Yahusha (Jesus) is telling the parable to the chief priests and elders, who had given the Father the public yes and withheld the obedience, which is hypocrisy as Sirach defines it: a performance for the watching crowd with nothing behind it. Take good heed what you speak, Sirach says, because the Father holds a man to what his mouth promised.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 1:29 — *Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men.* The second son's public yes and absent obedience at Matthew 21:30.

new_note: *Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men, and take good heed what you speak.* (Ecclesiasticus 1:29). *Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.* (Matthew 23:28). The word Yahusha (Jesus) uses, hypocrite, is the word for a stage actor, a man playing a part for an audience, and Sirach had warned against that very thing two centuries earlier: be not an hypocrite in the sight of men. Matthew 23:28 is where the seven woes land, outward righteousness for men to see, hypocrisy and iniquity underneath. The counsel in Sirach and the woe in Matthew describe one man, the one whose righteousness is aimed at human eyes. Yahuah (God) is not in the audience for that performance; he is reading the inside.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 1:29 — *Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men.* Righteousness outward unto men, hypocrisy within, at Matthew 23:28.

new_note: *Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men, and take good heed what you speak.* (Ecclesiasticus 1:29). *Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.* (Matthew 23:28). Sirach gives the counsel; Yahusha (Jesus) delivers the indictment of the men who ignored it. To be a hypocrite in the sight of men is to appear righteous unto men while being something else within, which is exactly how Matthew 23:28 reads. The warning came first, in a book the Reformation later cut from the library, and the Messiah's woe assumes his hearers should have known better. The religious system of his day had built itself on appearance; Sirach had told Yashar'el (Israel) long before that appearance is not what Yahuah (God) is weighing.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 1:29 — *Be not an hypocrite in the sight of men, and take good heed what you speak.* The Messiah's woe at Matthew 23:28 indicts exactly this man.

new_note: *My son, if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your soul for temptation.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:1). *And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.* (Matthew 10:22). Sirach opens his second chapter by telling the one who comes to serve Yahuah (God) to expect temptation and get his soul ready for it, and the next line says how: set your heart aright, and constantly endure. Yahusha (Jesus) sends the twelve out with the same preparation. They will be hated for his name, and the one who endures to the end is the one who is saved. Neither voice promises the servant an easy road; both tie the outcome to endurance. The disciple's endurance is not something new the gospel invented; it is what serving Yahuah (God) has always asked, and Sirach had been saying so for generations before the twelve were sent.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:1 — *if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your soul for temptation.* The endurance to the end Yahusha (Jesus) asks of the twelve at Matthew 10:22.

new_note: *My son, if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your soul for temptation.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:1). *Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.* (Matthew 26:41). In Gethsemane Yahusha (Jesus) tells the disciples to watch and pray so they do not enter into temptation, and they fall asleep. Sirach had said what they needed to hear before they ever came to the garden: if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your soul for temptation. The flesh is weak, the Messiah says; what Sirach adds is that a servant can get his soul ready for that weakness instead of being surprised by it. The disciples were willing in spirit and unprepared in soul, and the night proved Sirach right.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:1 — *My son, if you come to serve Yahuah (God), prepare your soul for temptation.* The watch and pray the sleeping disciples did not keep at Matthew 26:41.

new_note: *For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:5). *And ye shall be hated of all men for my name’s sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.* (Matthew 10:22). Sirach says the furnace is where acceptable men are proved, the way fire proves gold. Yahusha (Jesus) sends the twelve into that furnace with his eyes open: hated of all men for his name, and saved by enduring to the end. The hatred is not a sign the mission failed; it is the fire doing what fire does, and the disciple who comes through it is shown to be what Sirach calls acceptable. Adversity in the service of Yahuah (God) is the trial, not the verdict.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:5 — *gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.* The furnace the twelve are sent into at Matthew 10:22.

new_note: *For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:5). *And Peter remembered the word of Yahusha (Jesus), which said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly.* (Matthew 26:75). Peter went into the furnace that night and came out weeping. He had denied his Master three times, the cock crowed, the word came back to him, and he went out and wept bitterly. Sirach says acceptable men are tried in the furnace of adversity the way gold is tried in the fire, and the bitter weeping is the fire working. Caiaphas had rent his garments a few verses earlier (v.65); Peter rent his heart, which is the tearing Yahuah (God) asks for, and it carried him to the restoration by the shore in John 21. A disciple can fail, and a failed disciple is neither finished nor safe; he repents, and the furnace is what shows whether he is gold.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:5 — *acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.* Peter's denial and bitter weeping at Matthew 26:75 is the furnace doing its work.

new_note: *For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:5). *That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Yahusha HaMashiach (Jesus Christ):* (1 Peter 1:7). Peter writes to the scattered strangers with Sirach's figure in his hand: faith tried with fire, more precious than gold that perishes. Sirach had said gold is tried in the fire and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity, and Peter, who had been through that furnace himself the night the cock crowed, hands the picture on to the scattered seed of Yashar'el (Israel) he is writing to. The trial is not a sign of being forsaken; it is the proving, and what is proved is found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Yahusha HaMashiach (Jesus Christ). The Apocrypha and the apostle are describing the same furnace.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:5 — *gold is tried in the fire.* Peter's faith tried with fire at 1 Peter 1:7 is Sirach's figure handed on.

new_note: *Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and trust in him.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:6). *Trust in Yahuah (LORD), and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.* (Psalm 37:3). Sirach is repeating David. Believe in him, order your way aright, trust in him, is the same counsel as trust in Yahuah (LORD) and do good, the trusting and the doing bound together in one breath. Neither verse lets a man trust Yahuah (God) while walking however he pleases, and neither lets him order his way as if his own ordering were what held him up. The whole life leans on his help, and the leaning shows up as a way set aright.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:6 — *Believe in him, and he will help you; order your way aright, and trust in him.* David's *Trust in Yahuah (LORD), and do good* (Psalm 37:3), repeated.

new_note: *Saying, We will fall into the hands of Yahuah (God), and not into the hands of men: for as his majesty is, so is his mercy.* (Ecclesiasticus 2:18). *And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.* (Matthew 10:28). Those who fear Yahuah (God), Sirach says, would rather fall into his hands than into the hands of men, because his mercy is as great as his majesty. Yahusha (Jesus) gives the twelve the same choice with the stakes spelled out: men can kill the body and no more, while Yahuah (God) is able to destroy both soul and body in hell, so fear him and not them. Both verses move the fear off men and onto Yahuah (God), and both find that the safer place. The one whose hands hold the final judgment is the same one whose mercy matches his majesty, which is why falling into his hands is the choice of the one who fears him.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 2:18 — *We will fall into the hands of Yahuah (God), and not into the hands of men.* The fear moved off men and onto Yahuah (God) at Matthew 10:28.

new_note: *Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:1). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). Sirach begins his teaching on parents by speaking as a father: hear me, children, and do what I say, so that you may be safe. The whole chapter rests on the fifth commandment, the one Yahusha (Jesus) quotes back to the Pharisees in Matthew 15:4, honour thy father and mother, with the death penalty for cursing them attached. The tradition he is exposing in the verses that follow let a man vow to the altar what his aged parents needed and call himself free of them. Sirach had tied the children's safety to hearing and doing their father's word; the tradition untied it, and the Messiah names what Elohim (God) commanded to tie it back.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:1 — *Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.* The fifth commandment Yahusha (Jesus) quotes against the tradition at Matthew 15:4.

new_note: *Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter, that you may be safe.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:1). *But Yahusha (Jesus) said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 19:14). Sirach's picture of safety is children who hear their father and do what he says. Yahusha (Jesus) says the kingdom of heaven is of such, and he says it while his own disciples are forbidding the little ones to come. The kingdom belongs to children not because children are innocent but because a child hears his father's voice and comes when he is called; that is the disposition the kingdom is made of. Hearing is how the Father's children are shown to be his, and the one who hears and does thereafter is the one Sirach says will be safe.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:1 — *Hear me your father, O children, and do thereafter.* The children who come when called, of whom the kingdom is, at Matthew 19:14.

new_note: *He that fears Yahuah (God) will honour his father, and will do service to his parents, as to his masters.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:7). *For Moses said, Honour thy father and thy mother; and, Whoso curseth father or mother, let him die the death:* (Mark 7:10). Sirach binds honouring one's father to the fear of Yahuah (God): the man who fears him will serve his parents the way a servant serves his masters. Yahusha (Jesus) quotes the commandment behind that, for Moses said, honour thy father and thy mother, and then shows how the corban tradition severed what Sirach had joined, letting a man withhold from his parents what he vowed to the altar and call it devotion. A fear of Yahuah (God) that excuses a man from his parents is not the fear Sirach knew. The tradition had split the two apart; the Messiah puts Moses back on the table.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:7 — *He that fears Yahuah (God) will honour his father.* The commandment the corban tradition severs from the fear of Yahuah (God) at Mark 7:10.
flag: Regrade said NOT_FOUND only because the old note quoted the Mark verse first; the Sirach verse is 3:7 as labelled. Rebuilt in place, no move.

new_note: *Honour your father and mother both in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from them.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:8). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). Honour your parents both in word and deed, Sirach says, and the two words are the whole argument. The corban tradition Yahusha (Jesus) exposes in Matthew 15 kept the word and dropped the deed: a man could speak a vow that sounded devout while the support his father and mother needed was cut off by it. The Messiah answers with what Elohim (God) commanded, honour thy father and mother, with no room left for honour that is spoken and not done. Sirach had closed that gap generations before by naming both halves, and a tradition that keeps one half has kept neither.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:8 — *Honour your father and mother both in word and deed.* The word without the deed the corban tradition allowed, against Matthew 15:4.

new_note: *Honour your father and mother both in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from them.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:8). *And ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother;* (Mark 7:12). Mark 7:12 is the deed being forbidden: once the vow was spoken, the tradition suffered a man no more to do anything for his father or his mother. Sirach had said honour is both in word and deed, and the corban ruling kept the word, a vow formula that profited the system, and outlawed the deed. Measured by Sirach's own standard, the tradition did not merely fall short of the commandment; it subtracted half of it and called the remainder righteousness. Yahusha (Jesus) is not bringing a new standard against the elders, only the old one they had cut in two.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:8 — *both in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from them.* The deed the tradition forbids at Mark 7:12.

new_note: *For the blessing of the father establishes the houses of children; but the curse of the mother rooteth out foundations.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:9). *Making the word of Elohim (God) of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.* (Mark 7:13). Sirach says a father's blessing establishes the houses of children and a mother's curse roots out foundations, so honour toward parents is not a courtesy; it is what a house stands on. Yahusha (Jesus) says the tradition that voided the fifth commandment made the word of Elohim (God) of none effect, and Sirach tells you what that costs: the blessing forfeited and the foundation uprooted. A tradition that teaches sons to withhold from their parents is pulling the house down on them while calling it devotion. The Messiah names the voiding; Sirach had already named the price.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:9 — *the blessing of the father establishes the houses of children.* The foundation the tradition of Mark 7:13 roots out.
flag: Regrade said NOT_FOUND only because the old note quoted the Mark verse first; the Sirach verse is 3:9 as labelled. Rebuilt in place, no move.

new_note: *He that forsaketh his father is as a blasphemer; and he that angereth his mother is cursed: of Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:16). *And honour not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have ye made the commandment of Elohim (God) of none effect by your tradition.* (Matthew 15:6). Sirach does not treat neglect of parents as a small fault. To forsake a father is as blasphemy; to anger a mother is to be cursed of Yahuah (God). That is the weight behind Matthew 15:6, where a tradition lets a son honour not his father or his mother and call himself free, and the Messiah says the commandment of Elohim (God) has been made of none effect. What the tradition filed under devotion, Sirach had filed under blasphemy and curse. Yahusha (Jesus) is not inventing a harsher reading; he is reading the commandment the way the fathers already read it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:16 — *He that forsaketh his father is as a blasphemer.* The weight behind the voided commandment at Matthew 15:6.

new_note: *The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). *At that time Yahusha (Jesus) answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Yahuah (Lord) of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.* (Matthew 11:25). Sirach says favour before Yahuah (God) runs toward the one who humbles himself, and the greater he is, the lower he should go. Yahusha (Jesus) thanks the Father for the same thing working: these things hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed unto babes. The wise and prudent are the ones who did not humble themselves, who came to the Father with their standing in hand, and the revelation went past them to the ones with nothing to defend. Sirach names the principle; the prayer in Matthew 11 shows it happening.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:18 — *The greater you are, the more humble thyself.* Revealed unto babes, hidden from the wise and prudent (Matthew 11:25).

new_note: *The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). *And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 18:3). The greater you are, the more humble yourself, Sirach says, and Yahusha (Jesus) makes it the condition of entry: except you be converted and become as little children, you do not enter the kingdom at all. The disciples had just asked who is greatest, and the answer turned their measure upside down, because in the kingdom greatness is measured by how low a man will go, not how high he is set. Sirach was teaching it at a father's table long before the disciples argued about it on the road. The one who humbles himself as a little child is the greatest in that kingdom, which is exactly the favour Sirach said the humble find.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:18 — *The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* The humbling that is the kingdom's entry at Matthew 18:3.

new_note: *The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). *But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;* (Matthew 20:26). The kingdoms of the world run on domination; Yahusha (Jesus) has just said so of the princes of the Gentiles, and then he says it shall not be so among you. Whoever will be great among you, let him be your minister, the one who waits the table. Sirach had set the same direction centuries earlier: the greater you are, the more humble yourself, and favour before Yahuah (God) follows the humbling. In the kingdom greatness flows downward into service, the exact reverse of the kingdoms around it, and the Messiah is not introducing that reversal; he is restoring what the fathers had already taught and then living it out with a towel.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:18 — *the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* Greatness as service, against the domination of the princes, at Matthew 20:26.
flag: Kept 'Gentiles' from Matthew 20:25 as scripture has it. Dropped the old note's watcher-administration side-thread (Daniel 10, Ephesians 6) as beyond what the card needs.

new_note: *The greater you are, the more humble thyself, and you shall find favour before Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 3:18). *But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.* (Matthew 23:11). Sirach's counsel runs opposite to how religious status works: the greater you are, the more humble yourself. In Matthew 23 Yahusha (Jesus) is describing a leadership that had reversed it, loving the chief seats and the greetings and the titles, and in the middle of the woes he states the kingdom's rule: he that is greatest among you shall be your servant. Any system that climbs as it grows holy has walked Sirach backward. The favour before Yahuah (God) that Sirach promises goes to the one who goes down, and the Messiah says the same of greatness.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:18 — *The greater you are, the more humble thyself.* He that is greatest shall be your servant (Matthew 23:11).

new_note: *Many are in high place, and of renown: but mysteries are revealed to the meek.* (Ecclesiasticus 3:19). *At that time Yahusha (Jesus) answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Yahuah (Lord) of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.* (Matthew 11:25). Sirach says it as plainly as it can be said: many are in high place and of renown, but mysteries are revealed to the meek. Yahusha (Jesus) prays the same pairing to the Father, hidden from the wise and prudent, revealed unto babes. The meek in Sirach and the babes in Matthew are the same people, the ones with nothing to defend when the Father speaks, and the high and renowned are the same people as the wise and prudent, the ones whose standing fills the space where the hearing would be. The two verses line up in their shape, high against low, hidden against revealed, and they name one rule of how Yahuah (God) gives understanding.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 3:19 — *mysteries are revealed to the meek.* Hid from the wise and prudent, revealed unto babes (Matthew 11:25).

new_note: *My son, defraud not the poor of his living, and make not the needy eyes to wait long.* (Ecclesiasticus 4:1). *A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.* (Matthew 12:20). Sirach tells his son not to defraud the poor and not to make the needy eyes wait long; the next line adds not to make a hungry soul sorrowful or provoke a man in his distress. That is a description of handling the bruised reed without breaking it and the smoking flax without quenching it, which is what Isaiah said of the Messiah and what Matthew says Yahusha (Jesus) fulfilled. The disposition Sirach asks of a son is the disposition the Son carried. A system that sorts the bruised and the smoldering into categories and dismisses them has lost both the counsel and the Messiah who kept it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 4:1 — *defraud not the poor of his living, and make not the needy eyes to wait long.* The bruised reed not broken at Matthew 12:20, asked of the son first.

new_note: *My son, defraud not the poor of his living, and make not the needy eyes to wait long.* (Ecclesiasticus 4:1). *For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:* (Matthew 25:35). Sirach's command not to defraud the poor and not to keep needy eyes waiting is what the sheep in Matthew 25 are found to have done: I was hungry and you gave me meat, thirsty and you gave me drink, a stranger and you took me in. The judgment does not ask whether a man knew the right words; it asks what he did when the needy eyes were on him, and Sirach's chapter goes on to name the failure the goats are judged for, turn not away your eye from the needy (verse 5). This is not earning anything; it is what covenant life with Yahuah (God) looks like from the outside. The King recognizes his own by it because it was always his way.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 4:1 — *make not the needy eyes to wait long.* What the sheep are found to have done at Matthew 25:35.

new_note: *Reject not the supplication of the afflicted; neither turn away your face from a poor man.* (Ecclesiasticus 4:4). *A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.* (Matthew 12:20). Sirach is describing a face that stays turned toward the one in need, and Matthew 12:20 describes the Messiah's: a bruised reed he will not break, smoking flax he will not quench. The supplication of the afflicted is the bruised reed, and the poor man at the door is the smoking flax, easy to snap and easy to snuff. What Sirach asked of every son of Yashar'el (Israel), Yahusha (Jesus) did. A religious system that turns its face from the afflicted has abandoned the counsel and parted ways with the Messiah in the same motion.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 4:4 — *Reject not the supplication of the afflicted; neither turn away your face from a poor man.* The face the Messiah keeps toward the bruised reed at Matthew 12:20.

new_note: *Be as a father to the fatherless, and instead of an husband to their mother: so shall you be as the son of the Most High, and he shall love you more than your mother does.* (Ecclesiasticus 4:10). *For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.* (Matthew 12:50). Sirach says the man who fathers the fatherless and stands in for the widow's husband shall be as the son of the Most High, loved by him more than a mother loves. Yahusha (Jesus) says whoever does the will of his Father is his brother, sister, and mother. In both, the family of Elohim (God) is known by the doing of the Father's will, which in Sirach's example is the Torah's own care for the orphan and widow. The doing does not manufacture the sonship; it shows it, the way a son is known by bearing his father's likeness, and that is why Yahusha (Jesus) names his kin by it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 4:10 — *Be as a father to the fatherless, and instead of an husband to their mother.* The doing of the Father's will by which the family is known at Matthew 12:50.
flag: Theology adjustment: the old note read the doing as what 'makes' the doer a son of the Most High; rewritten so the doing reveals the family rather than creates it (hearing/doing reveals what was already true).

new_note: *He that holdeth her fast shall inherit glory; and wherever she entereth, Yahuah (God) will bless.* (Ecclesiasticus 4:13). *That I may cause those that love me to inherit substance; and I will fill their treasures.* (Proverbs 8:21). Wisdom speaks for herself in Proverbs: she causes those who love her to inherit, and she fills their treasures. Sirach describes the same inheritance from the receiving end: the one who holds her fast inherits glory, and wherever she enters, Yahuah (God) blesses. Both verses give wisdom an estate to leave, and both leave it to the ones who love her and will not let her go. Holding her fast is the inheritance's condition and its proof.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 4:13 — *He that holdeth her fast shall inherit glory.* Wisdom's inheritance for those who love her, Proverbs 8:21.
flag: Proverbs 8:21 (canon text) contains the word 'substance' (*inherit substance*); it is scripture and left as it reads.

new_note: *Strive for the truth to death, and Yahuah (God) shall fight for you.* (Ecclesiasticus 4:28). *Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.* (Matthew 10:32). Sirach tells his son to strive for the truth to death, and promises that Yahuah (God) will do the fighting. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the twelve that whoever confesses him before men will be confessed before the Father. Confessing him before men is the striving for the truth, carried all the way to death if it comes to that, and the confession before the Father is Yahuah (God) fighting for the one who did not let go. The promise in Sirach and the promise in Matthew are the same promise: the man who holds the truth in front of men is not left to hold it alone.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 4:28 — *Strive for the truth to death, and Yahuah (God) shall fight for you.* The confession before men that is confessed before the Father (Matthew 10:32).

new_note: *Instead of a friend become not an enemy; for thereby you shall inherit an ill name, shame, and reproach: even so shall a sinner that has a double tongue.* (Ecclesiasticus 6:1). *Then Judas, which betrayed him, answered and said, Master, is it I? He said unto him, Thou hast said.* (Matthew 26:25). Sirach warns against two things in one verse, the friend who turns enemy and the sinner with a double tongue, and Judas is both at the table. He had already sold his Master for thirty pieces of silver, and he asks, Master, is it I?, with the bargain in his pocket; that is the double tongue, one voice at the supper and another with the priests. Yahusha (Jesus) answers, thou hast said, and lets the man's own mouth carry the verdict. The betrayal served the Father's purpose and was Judas's own choice at the same time; the devil put it in his heart, John says, and Judas walked it out, and Sirach's warning stands over him as the shame and reproach of a friend who became an enemy.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 6:1 — *Instead of a friend become not an enemy.* Judas's *Master, is it I?* at Matthew 26:25 with the bargain already made.

new_note: *Be in peace with many: nevertheless have but one counsellor of a thousand.* (Ecclesiasticus 6:6). *A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.* (Proverbs 18:24). Solomon's proverb has two kinds of friend in it: the many a friendly man gathers, and the one who sticks closer than a brother. Sirach draws the same line and tells you how to count: be at peace with many, but take one counsellor out of a thousand. The crowd of friends is not the problem; letting the crowd counsel you is. Both writers are pointing at the rare one, the friend whose word you can build on, and both say you will not find him by being friendly to everyone but by proving him.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 6:6 — *have but one counsellor of a thousand.* The friend that sticketh closer than a brother of Proverbs 18:24.

new_note: *A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that has found such an one has found a treasure.* (Ecclesiasticus 6:14). *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:* (Matthew 13:45). Sirach says a faithful friend is a treasure, and the next verse says nothing countervails him; there is no price you could set against him. Yahusha (Jesus) says the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking goodly pearls who finds one worth everything he owns and sells all to have it. The merchant is Yahuah (God), and the pearl is the seed of promise — always the few, scattered like gold through the dust of the earth, and worth to him everything he has. Sirach knew that kind of worth in a friend; the Father knows it in his own, and when he finds them he does not haggle.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 6:14 — *he that has found such an one has found a treasure.* The one pearl worth all the merchant had, Matthew 13:45.

new_note: *For at the last you shall find her rest, and that shall be turned to your joy.* (Ecclesiasticus 6:28). *Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.* (Matthew 11:29). Sirach's sixth chapter is about putting the neck under wisdom's yoke; her fetters look like bondage at first, and at the last you find her rest, and the rest is turned to joy. Yahusha (Jesus) offers his yoke in the same words: take it, learn of me, and ye shall find rest unto your souls. The yoke is not the opposite of the rest; it is the road to it, in Sirach and in the Messiah alike. The pulpit offers a rest with no yoke in it, and the other side of the aisle calls the yoke a burden; both have lost what Sirach and the Messiah say in the same breath, that the rest is found at the end of wearing it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 6:28 — *at the last you shall find her rest, and that shall be turned to your joy.* The rest found under the yoke at Matthew 11:29.

new_note: *Seek not of Yahuah (God) preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:4). *And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues,* (Matthew 23:6). Sirach tells his son not to ask Yahuah (God) for preeminence or the king for the seat of honour. Matthew 23:6 describes a religious leadership that loved exactly those things, the uppermost rooms at feasts and the chief seats in the synagogues. The counsel and the woe are the same measure applied twice, once as a warning and once as a diagnosis, and the seat of honour is the tell in both. A system that wants the chief seat has made its religion a way of climbing, which is what Sirach said not to do with it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 7:4 — *Seek not of Yahuah (God) preeminence, neither of the king the seat of honour.* The chief seats loved at Matthew 23:6.

new_note: *Have you children? instruct them, and bow down their neck from their youth.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:23). *Then were there brought unto him little children, that he should put his hands on them, and pray: and the disciples rebuked them.* (Matthew 19:13). Sirach puts children on the list of a man's responsibilities: if you have them, instruct them and bend their necks from their youth. The parents in Matthew 19:13 are doing that when they bring their little ones to Yahusha (Jesus) for his hands and his prayer; it is the Torah's own charge to teach the children carried out in the plainest way, bringing them to the one who teaches. The disciples rebuked the parents, and the Messiah rebuked the disciples, because the bringing was right. Instruction begins with whom you bring your children to.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 7:23 — *Have you children? instruct them, and bow down their neck from their youth.* The parents bringing their children to Yahusha (Jesus) at Matthew 19:13.

new_note: *Honour your father with your whole heart, and forget not the sorrows of your mother.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:27). *For Elohim (God) commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.* (Matthew 15:4). Sirach says honour your father with your whole heart, and he adds the mother's sorrows so the son remembers what he cost her. Matthew 15:4 is the commandment behind it, honour thy father and mother, quoted by Yahusha (Jesus) against a tradition that let a son divide his heart, a vow to the altar in one half and nothing left for his parents in the other. Whole heart is Sirach's word against that division. Later in the same chapter the Messiah says what defiles comes out of the heart (vv.18–20), and the corban device is the proof: an honour split by a vow was defiled before the vow was spoken.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 7:27 — *Honour your father with your whole heart.* The whole heart the corban tradition divided, against Matthew 15:4.

new_note: *Love him that made you with all your strength, and forsake not his ministers.* (Ecclesiasticus 7:30). *Yahusha (Jesus) said unto him, Thou shalt love Yahuah Elohayka (the Lord thy God) with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.* (Matthew 22:37). Sirach is carrying the Shema forward: love him that made you with all your strength, the strength Deuteronomy 6:5 names and that Yahusha (Jesus) renders heart, soul, and mind when he gives the great commandment in Matthew 22:37. The Messiah is not replacing the commandments with love; he is quoting the commandment, the same one Sirach's readers recited twice a day. Sirach's next clause keeps love and Torah together, forsake not his ministers, and the verses around it give the priests their portion as it is commanded; loving Yahuah (God) with all your strength shows up as keeping what he commanded. That is the love written on the heart the prophets promised, not a feeling that excuses the walk.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 7:30 — *Love him that made you with all your strength.* The Shema the Messiah quotes at Matthew 22:37, carried forward by Sirach.
